The processing taxes, however, have

creasing the cost of living generally

AS pointed out in these dispatches

handed down its decision at Boston,
the processing taxes are really q levy

The advocates of the so-cailed export

The amazing thing is that anybody

should have thought the processing
tax could ever be upheld. The state
ment of the constitutional principle

in Boston is so clearly in line with
Supreme Court opinions that it is a

Here is the essential point in the
Circuit Court of Appeals decision, and
it can be read with the Gudey coal
bill in mind and its weird plan Of tax

THE power of Congress to regulate
Interstate Commerce does not auth
orize it to do so by taxing products

fore they enter interstate commerce,

merce.

ance of the general welfare but
whether Congress has any power to
control or regulate matters left to

Unwarranted Delegation.


Since Congress cannot delegate TO

originally possess, the processing tax

delegation of power. But even Il the
power were resident in Congress to
delegate the tax-making machinery,
standards and limits would have to
be set up to guard against arbitrary
and cap1icious action by Govern
ment department, and no such stand
ards were found by the court to exist

The Post Office Department is moving to break up "mail order divorces" offered to residents of this country through Mexican courts.

The first case of its kind on record, the department announced, resulted in issuance today of fraud order barring use of the mails to Francisco Arcovedo Guillermo, international counsellor at law at Merida, Yucatan, Mexico, who, it is shown, has been soliciting business in this country.

The opinion in the case, prepared by Solicitor Karl Crowley, and signed by Postmaster General James A. Farley, says: "A careful search of court decisions in numerous cases adjudicated in this country, shows that such alleged divorce DEGREES rendered by a foreign court wholly lacking in jurisdiction over the interested parties, are absolutely null and void and of no effect.

Persons remitting their money to this promoter are, therefore, defrauded of such amounts. In addition, persons relying on representations made by Guillermo and other mail order divorce specialists may be led to remarry and thus subject themselves to prosecution for bigamy. It is untrue to represent that such divorce DEGREES are necessarily recognized in the United States and must be held valid and conclusive in this country. Persons securing these so-called Mexican divorces through the mail from courts wholly lacking in jurisdiction are not restored to the status of unmarried persons, as represented by this promoter, the only place where such divorce DEGREES may be recognized being the state in which the court issuing such decree has jurisdiction."

Guillermo held out to his prospective clients that in Yucatan incompatibility, cruelty, desertion, insanity and mutual consent are grounds for divorce. There is no provision either for residence or domicile and none of the parties is required to appear personally, the whole thing being handled through power of attorney.

He contends that the divorces must be held as valid and conclusive in the United States and other foreign countries."

If you happen to step aboard ! street car to-day, taking the use of modern facilities of transportation as an every-day matter of course, you con give passing thought to the fact that exactly 100 years ago to-day the electric transportation system of the world consisted of a big idea in the head of country blacksmith and in a small model car which he held in his hands.

 The blacksmith was Thomas Davenport of Brandon, Vermont. Davenport was poor and unedu- cated but in years of struggle he made scores of electric motors, and at last, just 100 years ago in 1885, he saw one of his models roll forward on a circular track. He later exhibited a small car at Springfield and also at Boston. Davenport's principle was wrong, however, and his work was futile, but at least he had given the world an idea. To him America owes the honor of having originat- ed electric traction.

 Three years later, the first cleo trio car to run on standard gauge track was produced in Scot land. It was not until 1881, how ever, that Pacinnoti invented the reversible continuous current dyna- mo upon which all modern gener- 'ators and motors are based. The intervening 26 years between Day. export and Pacinnoti had been largely wasted as far as electric railway progress was concerned. Now came another similar interval, this time of IS years, before the first practical electric line was or- erated, and then nine more years before the construction of electric roads on q commercial scale was begun in Richmond, Va, by the late Frank J. Sprague, since named "the Father of the Electric Railways"

 The Richmond line, the first in- stance of commercial electric rail- way traction in history, began op :. eration in February, 1888. Three months later in May, 1888, Con- necticut had the honor of witness ing what is believed to be the first use of electric traction for the transportation of freight. The car was run in the lower Naugatuck Valley near Ansonia and Derby. On its first run, the car was found to be too high to pass under a low bridge and two months had to be spent cutting it down before it could be put into full-time opera tior, carrying freight between docks on the river and industrial plants in the valley sector. Just ten years before this, an experi- ment in the street car traction had been made by Henry Bushnell on Whitney avenue in New Haven, in which a compressed air motor was used to provide locomotion.

 Electric railway lines grew rap idly in Connecticut, most of them to be combined near the dawn of the century under the name, The Consolidated Company, and later under the name, The Connecticut Company.

farmers for that portion of the crop
which is sold abroad at lower than
the domestic prices.


"Dumping" Contemplated.


The plan contemplates dumping
of wheat, or cotton or other farm
products in foreign nations at prices
perhaps considerably below the prices
for such commodities in the United
States. It is not expected that wheat
will be dumped, it is said, in countries
which produce that grain. But the
dumping of the wheat may be made
in countries which are neutral,
countries which import wheat. It may
be that it will be a necessary complement to this plan to enter upon
unilateral trade agreements with
foreign nations to carry it through
successfully. In other words, treaties
may be made with individual nations
to take so much American wheat, or
cotton, for concessions made
individually with each nation to take
some of their products.


It would be a strange shift from the
earlier Republican position on this
question of farm aid to find the equalization fee written into the party's
national platform. The Republicans
who favor this plan say it would get
away from governmental "regimentation" of the farmers, and at the same
time would provide means of check
ing unwise production. The farmer
would make his own odds in this
gamble. The Republicans insist it is
unthinkable that the country shall
continue indefinitely on the pillow
under system of the A. A. A., with
Government checks to the farmers for
land not used for specific crops and
processing taxes on the crops when
they are placed in the hands of the
producers.


May Accept Some Laws.


The Republicans may accept some
of the New Deal legislation and not
campaign against it, just as they ac-
cepted the Federal Reserve Act and
the Federal Trade Commission Act
written during the Wilson administra-
tion. For example, the laws for bank
deposit insurance, the law creating a
commission to deal with securities and
the stock exchange, the projected
economic security law, which will pro-
vide for old-age pensions and unem-
ployment insurance, and several others
enacted during the Roosevelt admins-
tration are likely to be tacitly accepted
by the Republicans in the coming
campaign.


However, G. O. P. leaders believe
that plenty of issues will be at hand
when the time comes, issues made by
the Democrats themselves. These
leaders are still puzzling their heads
over the selection of nominees for
President and Vice President. The
grass roots convention in Springfield
was not intended to develop candi-
dates, nor did it so, outwardly at
least. A little less than a year in
advance of the national convention,
it looks as though the convention
would meet with a lot of "favorite
son" candidates on hand, and per-
haps with a considerable number of
uninstructed State delegations. In
such a convention almost anything
might happen. A speech that took
the convention on its feet might be
the turning point, just as in the
Democratic national convention which
nominated Bryan in 1896.


How soon and to what extent the
various presidential possibilities will
become active candidates remains to
be seen. A number of States hold
presidential preferential primaries
next year. These may bring out a
crop of open candidates. In the
meantime, most of the "possibilities"
deny that they are candidates.
They hold that for the present this
is the wiser course.

and bouncing over the boulder strewn
road or through the deep ruts that

innate buying.

work for and to own.
